Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead) moved the second reading of Bill No. 28, to amend the Bankruptcy Act (Priority of Claims).
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.
On section 1-Priority of claims for wages, salaries and commissions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Explain.

Mr. Chairman, bankruptcy offers a method as well as a means for distributing among his creditors the property of a man who is unable to pay his debts in full. According to the act, creditors are divided into two classes, ordinary and preferred. Among the preferred creditors are servants who work for a salary. That class

Bankruptcy Act-Priority of Claims
has always been recognized as being entitled to preferential treatment and to be paid their wages for a period of three months preceding a winding-up order. The purpose of this amendment is to provide for a class of servants hitherto unprovided for. A large number of salesmen receive their renumeration for their work either when the goods sold have been delivered, or have been paid for, or at some fixed time after either events. Travelling salesmen are now going throughout the provinces selling goods to be delivered next autumn, and most of them will receive payment for their efforts thirty, sixty and ninety day after the goods have been delivered or after they have been paid for. The purpose of this amendment is to entitle these men to preference for their wages when a period of not more than three months has elapsed from the date their wages became due. If a salesman were to sell a bill of goods to be delivered on January 1st, and under the terms of his contract he is to receive his salary, wages, commission or whatever you choose to call it, thirty days after the goods are paid for, and the goods were to be paid for on March 1, he would have a preferred claim should the firm for whom he is working happen to go into bankruptcy within three months after March 1.
That is not now the case.

No. But there is
nothing new in the principle involved. There are forty odd thousand, travelling salesmen in this country who are denied the benefit of a preference for their wages falling due during the three months which precede a bankruptcy. This amendment seeks to give to that large class the privilege extended to others.

Mr. Chairman, I have no
antagonism to the principle of this bill except that I find that it will give to these men working on commission a double priority. They will be given priority for the three months following the date of the assignment, but there will be commissions falling due before that from previous transactions or possibly cash sales-these men do not sell exclusively on a basis of payment in three months; sometimes they sell for cash-and they would be given priority for the three months prior to the date of assignment as well as a further three months following the assignment.

I do not think that that would happen. After earning their commissions some of these men have to wait from
six months to a year before receiving them. There might be cash transactions within the three months preceding bankruptcy which would entitle them to preferential payment.

And earnings falling due
within that period.

Yes. At the proper
time an amendment to this section will be offered.
Is there any such thing as a legal definition of the term "travelling salesman"?

I merely took that class as an example. The section of the bill reads as follows:
Thirdly, all wages, salaries, commissions or compensation of any clerk, servant, travelling salesman, labourer or workman, in respect of services rendered to the bankrupt or assignor during three months before the date of receiving order or assignment:

Will the hon. member explain the necessity for the words:
-moreover, that any advances made on account of such commission shall be deemed to have been legally paid on account thereof;

The Bankruptcy Act
provides that certain payments made within thirty or sixty days prior to a bankruptcy are presumed to have been made in anticipation of bankruptcy and are therefore illegal. An exception is made in the case of wages, and this section would put the payment of commissions in the same class and exempt them from the presumption of fraud which attaches to ordinary payments made in anticipation of bankruptcy.
I would point out to the hon. member that if he desires to make any amendment, this is the appropriate time.

I move:
That the word "or" in the eighteenth and twenty-first lines be deleted and the words "or payment" be added in the eighteenth line after the word "delivery" and the words "or paid for'' be added in the twenty-first line after the word "delivered."

I would like to point out that
the hon. member cannot amend his own bill.
I move that amendment

Would the introducer of the bill be kind enough to read it as it will be when amended, beginning with the words "provided that commission."?
1654	COMMONS
Bankruptcy Act-Priority of Claims

It will read:
Provided that commission earned more than three months before the date of a receiving order or assignment, but not payable (by the terms of the creditor's agreement) until the shipment, delivery or payment of the goods sold, shall be deemed to have been earned within three months of the date of the receiving order or assignment, when the said goods have been shipped, delivered or paid for within three months of the receiving order or assignment.

Would the hon. member in
charge of the bill not think it better if it read: "delivery of or payment for the goods sold"? It is better English anyway.
I think the hon. member's point is well taken.
Yes-"Shipment, delivery of or payment for."

The hon. member for
Comox-Alberni a few minutes ago raised a point that was not cleared up, at least to my satisfaction, and that is whether there might not be more than three months' priority. Suppose a travelling salesman were working on a cash basis during the last three months before bankruptcy. He would receive priority for his full time for those three months. Then if commissions fell due for previous transactions, he really might be crowding into those last three months much more than three months' priority. Is that not correct?

I think that is correct,
but that is exactly where the difficulty lies, that people who work for those commissions are precluded from payment for six, nine or twelve months, and in that event the man would be receiving merely what he would have received months before had he been receiving a daily, weekly or monthly stipend. This is a peculiarity of the commission arrangement.	'

I understand that, but there is a possibility, under this amendment, that he may be getting priority for much more than three months' pay for his work. Is that not correct? Let me put the case again, because I doubt whether the sponsor of the bill understood it before. This is the case I have in mind; Suppose a travelling salesman were working on a cash basis, getting paid day by day for what he does-that might or might not be possible-during the last three months before bankruptcy. Under the bill as it stands he gets priority for three months' remuneration. Then, under the proposed amendment he also gets priority for such commissions as may fall due during 
those three months for work that he has done six, nine or twelve months previously. In other words, in the case I have put, he gets a priority that an ordinary wage earner does not receive. There may be some explanation. The point has just occurred to me.

That is quite correct,
bpt I do not know that it is altogether a likely case. Let us suppose that a man were working on commission, he might finish his work at the end of May, his commissions might not fall due until early next year. On June 1 he goes to work on a cash basis for someone else. The situation would be identical, but still, under the amendment, he would preserve his right to priority in the event of bankruptcy to all commissions falling due within three months of a receiving order.

In that case he would have
lost his right of*priority, would he not? Does the law not require the man to be in the employ of the bankrupt right up to the date of the assignment?

The amendment would
give him that priority.
Why should the commission man be preferred in any way to the ordinary wage earner who may have earned wages over a period of, say, a year before the assignment?

He is not. He comes in as an ordinary employee. The only difference is that under this system the man, instead of receiving wages, weekly, fortnightly or monthly, has to wait six, nine or twelve months for his commission. This merely gives him a priority in regard to amounts which fell due within the three months preceding a receiving order.

That is exactly what the bill does not say. It does not say a priority for three months' earnings. It says, "commission earned more than three months before." He might earn twelve months' commission and it is all to be considered as coming in under the three months' priority. That priority should be limited at least to three months' earnings of commissions. Now he can get priority for twelve months' earnings.

Only if the commission
falls due within the three months.

I think the difference between the commission man as dealt with in the bill and the ordinary wage earner is this, that the ordinary wage earner can sue for his wages that have been earned prior to the three months, as soon as they have been earned, whereas the commission man is tied

Criminal Code-Trade Marks
up; he cannot sue. In other words, he may have earned his commission and he may see his employer going on the rocks, but his hands are tied by reason of the agreement that his commission is not to be paid until the goods are delivered or paid for. He has absolutely no protection. In other words, he is in quite a different position from the wage earner who can take immediate summary proceedings to cover his wages earned prior to the three months; the commission man cannot do so.

The commissions of the commission man, I presume, are falling in from month to month and he is being paid commissions from time to time throughout the year. This amendment will permit him to get commissions which have been earned beyond the three months period, 'but not payable before the three months period. That will mean that he has priority over the claims that fall in during the three months prior to the assignment and also will have priority for the commissions that have been earned, say, during the twelve months before that. The commissions have been earned but are not payable. By way of illustration an ordinary farm labourer who is working for a period, say, of eight months, and is to be paid in the fall, has priority for only three months' wages. Suppose he works eight .months at $40 a month, payable in the fall; he has priority for only three months' wages.
He can sue for his wages.
He cannot sue until his wages become due, which may be at a date after t'he assignment. This commission man has clearly a preference over the ordinary wage earner.

It seems to me that a number of hon. members are labouring under a misapprehension. If they will refer to line 21 and following lines of the amending bill they will see that it is limited to the goods which have been shipped or delivered within three months of the receiving order or assignment. Surely it cannot be contended that the preference amounts to more than the commission on the goods shipped in the last three months prior to the assignment.
There .might have been a whole summer's trade done in the three months.

That might accidentally
happen.

subtopic: FORGING OF TRADE MARKS-SALE OF GOODS FALSELY MARKED
speechtext:
This bill is introduced at.
the request of certain persons who have been interested in the protection of trade marks, whether used as labels or in any other way in which a trade mark is used. The right to the use of a trade mark is for the protection of the person owning the trade mark and applying it to goods of his manufacture. If that trade mark be allowed to be reproduced and applied to goods which are not of his manufacture the manufacturer is being deprived of his rights, and at the same time goods, possibly of an inferior quality, are being imposed upon the'public by some manufacturer other than the one in rightful possession of the trade mark. I understood from those who asked me to promote this legislation that section 486 of the criminal code was not clear enough to enable a conviction to be had for an infraction of such section 486. It was found that if a man had trade marks and packages together in his premises obviously with the intention of applying the trade mark to the packages and going into the market with the substituted goods, he could not be convicted unless it was proved he himself forged the trade mark. If he had the forgeries prepared by others and only had the- forged trade mark in his possession, there was no offence. Moreover it was found that unless he had actually applied the trade mark or label to the package there was no offence under the code. It was quite obviously the intention that no one should secure forged trade marks and packages which were designed to carry a certain trade mark and place himself in a position whereby he could issue goods of a spurious nature deceiving the public as to the true source of manufacture. In a good many industries matters have come to a serious pass and I understand the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) agrees that this legislation will remedy the fault which now exists under section 486. The proposal is that the section should have added to it in the second line of section (a) the words "or reproduces in any manner." I am quite frank to say that the unsatisfactory condition of the law in regard to trade marks has created some havoc in a good many rather popular industries; at least it is creating difficulties among the consumers of certain of the manufactures of those industries.

When the committee

speechtext:
No, Washington. My right hon. friend suggested that he had been transferred to London. I think that is an improper term to use. The truth is the order in council was passed on July 24, 1930, appointing Mr. Massey to London. It is not correct to say that he was appointed to London in the month of May or any other date, because the order in council was dated, as I say, July 24, 1930. It was approved on that day, the order being passed the day before. It reads:
The committee of the privy council, on the recommendation of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, advise that the Honourable "V iucent Massey, a member of His Majesty's Privy Council for Canada, be appointed High Commissioner for Canada in London from the 23rd July, 1930, under the act, chapter 92 of the revised statutes of 1927, in succession to the Honourable Peter C. Larkin, deceased; and that his duties include supervision over the various agencies of the Canadian government in the United Kingdom as described in the order in council (P.C. 330, 10th February, 1922) by which Mr. Larkin was appointed.
The committee, on the same recommendation, further advise that His Majesty the King in respect of Canada be humbly moved to issue Mr. Massey's letter of recall from the United States, and to indicate that Mr. Massey has fulfilled his mission to the entire satisfaction of His Majesty in respect of Canada.
That was the order in council which removed Mr. Massey from Washington and appointed him to London. I said it removed him from Washington; that is hardly a correct term. It asked that his letters of recall be granted, and as a matter of fact the way in which a minister is withdrawn is not by order in council. He has his letters of recall signed by the sovereign on the application of the government affected, and in this instance the letters of recall were actually signed on the day this government came into office. They subsequently came back to Ottawa from London; they were signed on the 7th day of August, 1930, so on the 23rd of July Mr. Massey was appointed, the approval being given on the succeeding day, and his letters of recall were actually signed by the sovereign on the 7th of August of last year.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I think not. The order in council appointing Mr. Larkin, to which reference has been made, contained these words:
The minister considers that this is an appropriate ^ occasion for defining the duties of the Canadian High Commissioner. The statute creating this office (43 Vie. chap 11) provides that the high commissioner should act as the duly accredited representative of Canada and resident agent of the Dominion in London to watch over the growing interests of Canada in the United Kingdom. The policy embodied m the original act creating this office has been departed from in that there are in London at the present time direct representatives, having practically independent and separate offices, of the Departments of Immigration, Trade and Commerce, Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment and Board of Pension Commissioners, also other departmental representatives carrying on their work outside the control of the High Commissioner.
The minister submits-
That is my right hon. friend opposite.
-that there is necessity in this connection to coordinate these activities, and prevent overlapping. It has frequently happened that the same matters were dealt with by different offices and agencies at the same time, thus producing confusion and injury to Canada's reputation and the effectiveness of its administrative methods.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs therefore, both on the grounds of economy and efficiency, and with the concurrence of the ministers concerned, recommends that all the official activities of the various agencies of the Canadian government in the United Kingdom should be placed under the supervision of the high commissioner.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs further recommends that the high commissioner should in all matters of public policy communicate direct with the Prime Minister.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendations and submit the same for approval.
That order in council was passed on February 10, 1922, and reference was made to that order in council in express terms when Mr. Massey was appointed on the 23rd of July, 1930. It is the basis of the observation I made last session, that the high commissioner must be taken to be practically a member of the administration. Mr. Larkin was sworn of the privy council shortly after his appointment. Mr. Ferguson was sworn of the privy council. It was felt that one who is charged with the responsibility for the conduct not of one but of several departments of the public service in London must occupy a position' almost analogous to that of a member of the government, and he is so treated. Now, for instance, in the office at London at the present time 3rou will find lodged the high commissioner, the immigration office, a branch of the Departments of Trade and Commerce, Agriculture,

Supply-External Affairs
Customs, Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment and Secretary of State, and there are also branches of the Archives and the air force in other offices.
The result is that to all intents and purposes the High Commissioner for Canada is minister in London, apart from being high commissioner, for immigration, trade and commerce, agriculture, customs, soldiers' civil reestablishment and secretary of state. I say to this committee that during all the time Mr. Massey was in the United States he discharged no duties analogous to these at all, and no minister from this country to Tokyo or Paris discharges any such duties or exercises any such oversight in connection with the activities of Canada in those countries. There is such a clear distinction that all you have to do is go into the offices and observe them. I did say to Mr. Massey that I thought he had discharged his duties at Washington with credit and distinction alike to himself and to this country, but he discharged what might be called the ornamental duties which appertain to the office of minister. For instance, he had a commercial attache, Mr. Mahoney, at Washington, who looked after these matters in that city. That cannot be said in any sense to be analogous to the departmental activities of our representative in London, and in the duties discharged so effectively by Mr. Massey, the social obligations of a great office in Washington, he had nothing analogous to these duties which must be discharged by wnom-ever is the high commissioner in London, because these branches of the departments of government of this country which are under that roof in London must be administered by the high commissioner.
Sir Alexander Galt was the first high commissioner from this country. He was appointed to London by Sir John A. Macdonald. Part of the correspondence between Macdonald and Galt has been published. Part of it will be found in the letters of Sir John A. Macdonald; part will be found in the life of Sir Alexander Galt, and part has not been published at all. There is no doubt, however, that while on the one hand Sir John Macdonald regarded Sir Alexander Galt as a Canadian ambassador, on the other hand he treated him as reflecting the mind of his government, and he was very clear in that regard. Then there came Sir Charles Tupper. Would anyone for a moment say that had the government of the day been defeated. Sir Charles Tupper could have remained in London representing a Liberal government
in Canada? Has anyone ever taken the trouble to read the debates in this house showing the attitude of the Liberal party towards Sir Charles Tupper and his administration of the affairs of Canada as high commissioner in London? Would anyone for a moment say he would have been accepted as high commissioner had the Liberal government succeeded in the days of Mr. Blake, or later in the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier? When Sir Donald Smith, afterwards Lord Strathcona, was appointed to succeed Sir Charles Tupper at London, it will be recalled that Sir Charles Tupper came to Canada to take over the position of Prime Minister. He came over as the Conservative Prime Minister. Previously he had come to Canada to participate in a general election; he took part in that election and then returned to his office as high commissioner. The relations between him and Sir John A. Macdonald were of such a character that they are well described by the mention of that famous cablegram which Sir John Macdonald sent to him, saying that the situation was getting rather complicated and his presence here was greatly desired. Sir Charles Tupper cabled, "Sailing to-morrow," and he came to Canada and took part in the election. Then he went back and remained as high commissioner until he came out to Canada as Prime Minister. Following that, Sir Donald Smith, afterwards Lord Strathcona, was made high commissioner.
While Sir Donald Smith was high commissioner, the general election of 1911 took place. Lord Strathcona came out and offered his resignation both to Sir Wilfrid Laurier and to Sir Robert, then Mr. Borden. Neither accepted it. The one said it was not for him to accept it and the other said he was not yet in a position to do so, and he remained there as high commissioner until he died. But it is also known that Lord Strathcona, at a public banquet on Dominion day in London, indicated that he proposed to retire from the office. It is well known that his successor was selected and was named, in so far as a successor could be named without its being made public. That is well known. His position was an extraordinary one. He was a man of advanced years when appointed, a man of great wealth, and he occupied a position that could not be said in any sense to be political. He discharged his duties without regard to the government, by merely carrying into effect the instructions he received. Those who are familiar with the work he did then will realize that the office at 19 Victoria street was an entirely
Supply-External Affairs

different place from Canada House on Trafalgar square to-day, both from the standpoint of the work that had to be done, the personnel and the staff employed, and from the point of view of the general attitude which a high commissioner must observe towards the problems that come before him for consideration.
When Lord Strathcona vacated the office the Right Hon. Sir George Perley occupied it; and during a portion of that time, be it known, he was a member of Sir Robert Borden's government. There are those who believe that it is in the interests of this country and of Great Britain as well that the incumbent of that office should be a member of the government of the day in this country. I know that Sir George Perley entertained that opinion and still does, and there are many who share the 'view. It will be recalled that when Sir George Perley surrendered the office he offered his resignation to my right hon. friend opposite and in due course retired. I do not say that, had he desired to remain, the right hon. gentleman might not have permitted him to do so; but I should be inclined to say he would not. It would not have been his view at that time that the High Commissioner in London should be a former member of a Conservative administration. And indeed, I have always felt-there is nothing new about this -that he would have been entirely right in viewing the situation in that light. Then came the success of my right hon. friend opposite, and with the retirement of Sir George Perley, Mr. P. C. Larkin was appointed high commissioner. Mr. Larkin was a gentleman of large business experience and interests, and he discharged his duties well. But certainly, from any conversations which he ever had with me, I do not think he would have looked upon the office as a political one. He did indicate, however, that had the party with which I was associated been successful in 1925 or 1926 he would have resigned. Whether his resignation would have been accepted or not is, of course, a matter with which the government of that day would have had to deal.
Then Mr. Larkin died and the office fell vacant. Mr. Pa-caud, as acting commissioner, has discharged the duties of the office, one of very considerable importance, just as he would normally have discharged them had he been merely secretary. He was appointed acting commissioner and was given a small additional compensation. I may say that he did not receive the emoluments and fees that were
fMr. Bennett.}
paid the commissioner, although he discharged the duties. Then, the office having been vacant from 1929 until July, 1930, Mr. Massey, who was then minister at Washington, was appointed to the post. It well may be that had the post been started on the basis which my right hon. friend mentions it could have been maintained as a diplomatic position. But I think I have indicated sufficient to any hon. member of this house to show that, according to the records of Hansard and the history of the period during which the gentlemen named were high commissioners, in every instance these gentlemen were, shall I say, colleagues, in the large and broad sense, of the Prime Minister and his ministers of the respective governments. And when Mr. Massey found himself in the position he did-and I am free to say that I had no knowledge that action had been taken until after I saw the order in council under which he was appointed, of which, naturally, I was not aware in view of the fact that we did not come into office until August 7-is it not apparent to the house, under these circumstances, that Mr. Massey would be the last man in the world to expect to remain as high commissioner in London?
It is common knowledge in Washington, as it is elsewhere, that Mr. Massey felt perfectly certain that the then government would be sustained. Had he remained at Washington he would not have been dealt with differently from Mr. Marler or Mr. Roy. These gentlemen are still occupying their positions as ministers, and Mr. Marler is a former member of a Liberal administration. He occupies the office in Tokyo and is at present on leave of absence in Canada. He has not been removed from his office, and it has not 'been suggested that he should be. He is still there. Mr. Roy was a former Liberal senator, appointed for Alberta in 1905, a Liberal 'by conviction and declaration-indeed, I should say, by warm declarations in recent years. But Mr. Roy occupies his position still and no one questions it. No one has suggested that Mr. Marler should resign. I have not done so. Nor has anyone suggested that Mr. Roy should resign; I have not, nor has the government. These gentlemen are both in the positions to which they were appointed.
But I do draw a sharp distinction between a minister and one who occupies the statutory position of high commissioner, as a civil servant charged with administrative responsibility for a given department of the public service of Canada in London. And for that reason I believe that Mr. Massey felt it was clearly his duty to resign, as in fact he did.

Supply-External Affairs
I can only say that the same considerations that moved the government with respect to the positions of Mr. Marler and of Mr. Roy would undoubtedly have moved the administration with respect to Mr. Massey had he remained at Washington. The situation is so entirely different in a foreign country from what it is in Great Britain: it involves so many different problems, so many different angles from which the same problem may be viewed, that I cannot conceive of any Canadian occupying the position of high commissioner who does not command at once the confidence, in the widest sense, of the ministry of the day. He reports directly to the Prime Minister in accordance with the minute which was passed when Mr. Larkin was appointed, and he gives his confidence to the Prime Minister. Mr. Massey was the first to realize the situation, and so resigned.
There is the story, and I am confident, as confident as one can be, that no man can properly discharge the duties of high commissioner who has not, in the large, broad and true sense of the term, that confidence in the policies of the administration which has appointed him, which will enable him successfully to fulfil the functions of his office. For that reason the resignation of Mr. Massey was accepted. And I am bound to say that a high commissioner's resignation would foe accepted again to-morrow; and so long as the administration holds the views it now holds, that action must be taken should1 a similar situation arise at any time.
But let us test the question in another way. Will my right hon. friend say that if he were in office to-morrow he would not expect the present high commissioner to tender him his resignation? It seems to me that one must always test these questions by some practical inquiry.

I have done that by appealing to the record of history; because I have had to accept responsibility I have not suddenly arrived at an opinion with respect to it. From the opinion which I have held since I first knew of this office I was able to appreciate its historical record. My right hon. friend has spoken about an informant. If the statement made by the Prime Minister is correct, whoever was his informant told him something that was not true. When my right hon. friend refers to an informant, he owes it to the house to give the name of his informant.
What I wish to say, however, is this: my right hon. friend before the six o'clock recess indulged in a personal attack upon a distinguished gentleman in public life who was not in the house or in any way in a position to defend himself. I shall give again to the house on his behalf the only statement which it is within my power to give, namely, the one contained in that gentleman's communication to the Prime Minister himself. It is in a letter which I read this afternoon under date of August 14, 1930, and the point at issue is contained in the following sentence :
In our discussion on this subject you were good enough to make clear your view that the office of high commissioner should be held by someone in close political association with the government of the day, and I understood from what you said that you had in mind plans for this post as a result of "which my own appointment could no longer stand.
As a result of the plans which the Prime Minister himself indicated to Mr. Massey, the latter's appointment could no longer stand. For this reason he continues:
In these circumstances, I, of course, at once offered you my resignation from the high com-rmssionership, which I now confirm.
May I say that if there ever was a gentleman who filled a public office in a manner which was acceptable to men and women of all political parties in this country, it was the Hon. Vincent Massey in the distinguished manner in which he filled the position of the first minister from this country to Washington. Not only did Mr. Massey win the

Supply-External Affairs
praise of men of all political parties in Canada, but distinguished public men and officiils of the highest rank from Great Britain were loud in their praises of the services which Mr Massey had rendered not only to Canada but to the British Empire. During the time Mr. Massey was at Washington we _ had .visiting Canada two British prime ministers, at least one secretary of state for foreign affairs and we have had visits from two British ambassadors who were his associates at Washington. All of these very distinguished gentlemen have been more than loud in their praise of the great service which was being rendered at Washington by Mr. Massey not only to Canada but to the British Empire as a whole. It is generally admitted that no minister or ambassador at Washington filled his position with greater credit to himself and the country which he represented there than did the Hon. Mr. Massey. In these circumstances it was owing to Mr. Massey to receive rather the public thanks of the Prime Minister of Canada for the services which he had rendered, than the personal attack which was directed against him just before the six o'clock recess. My right hon. friend, however, has evidently upon reflection thought better of his words and he has seen well this evening to intimate that with his own lips he told Mr. Massey he had represented his country most acceptably during the time he represented Canada at Washington.
But I must take exception to the view expressed by the Prime Minister as to the significance of the position of minister at Washington. The Prime Minister said that Mr. Massey had fulfilled certain ornamental duties; that he had discharged social functions will great satisfaction and credit. If the Prime Minister thinks the position of minister at Washington is one concerned pi i-marilv with ornamental duties and social functions, he has an entirely erroneous view of what the position of minister at Washington amounts to. I hope he has taken other things into consideration in connection with that appointment than the merely ornamental duties and social functions that are to be performed. The right hon. Lord Bryce, who was British ambassador at Washington for many years, stated on one of his visits to Ottawa that two-thirds of the business of the British ambassador at the time he occupied that office was concerned with all-important affairs with respect to Canada. Later Sir Esme Howard, who was British ambassador at Washington at the time Mr. Massey went there, made a similar statement. Sir
[Mr. Mackenzie Kine.3
Esme Howard indicated that the duties of the Canadian minister at Washington were most extensive and responsible. With a neighbour as near as the United States is to this Dominion, with border questions of the character they are, with the extent of territory what it is, there are in the nature of things any number of all-important questions. Let us take a matter such as the St. Lawrence waterways: does my right hon. friend think that matters pertaining to the St. Lawrence waterways are in the nature of an ornamental duty or a social obligation: that it requires one possessed only of those qualifications to handle matters of that kind? Then there are questions with respect to deportations, to emigration matters to the tariff and what not. There is n-o end of all-important questions. Indeed, it would be very difficult to imagine two countries that have more important questions arising between them than those which arise and are certain to continue to arise between the United States and Canada. What is required in a minister representing Canada at Washington are the very highest of qualifications of a character that would be expected from one holding an all-important position in public life.
My right hon. friend spoke about the different distinguished gentlemen who have held the position of High Commissioner in London. In that connection it seemed to me his remarks served only to emphasize the difference between the point of view the Conservative party is now taking through the Prime Minister and the point of view the Liberal party has always taken. My right hon. friend pointed out that Sir Charles Tup-per was a strong political controversialist; that Sir Alexander Galt had equally been very strong politically as a controversialist. He did not need to point out the controversial powers of the present High Commissioner, but he altogether skipped over mention of the fact that during the entire time that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was Prime Minister of Canada, the position of High Commissioner in London was held by Lord Strathcona who was a political opponent. For many years, including the fifteen years of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's administration Lord Strathcona continued to occupy the position of High Commissioner in London long after Sir Alexander Galt had filled it, after Sir Charles Tupper had filled it and prior to the time Sir George Perley filled it. Lord Strathcona was not discharging merely an ornamental function in London; he was not acting on his own initiative in matters over there, with the

Supply-External Affairs
Canadian government indifferent to what was transpiring in London. Lord Strathcona was acting under the direction of the government of Canada : he was the agent of the government of Canada and he was fulfilling his duties under the direction and in accordance with the instructions of the Prime Minister of the day. During the time that Lord Strathcona held the position of high commissioner many very important negotiations were conducted between the Canadian and British governments. Though himself a conservative, he reflected the mind of the Liberal administration in his negotiations with the British Government just, as I said this afternoon, Lord Crewe, who had been a member of the Liberal government in Great Britain, reflected the mind of a Conservative cabinet when he was ambassador in Paris; just as Lord Bryce, when he was ambassador at Washington, reflected during a part of his term of office the mind of a Conservative cabinet, although he himself had previously been a member of a Liberal administration in England. The point of view which Sir Wilfrid Laurier took throughout the whole of his administration was that Lord Strathcona had filled the position acceptably prior to the time that he Sir Wilfrid had come into office; that he was a gentleman whose name, ability and influence were recognized, that it was in the interest of Canada in its relations with the British government to maintain every confidence between the government there and the government here, and that Lord Strathcona, being a public man and broad in his views, might be expected to discharge his duties as high commissioner in an acceptable manner, and he did discharge them in a most acceptable manner during the entire time he was Canada's High Commissioner.
My right hon. friend asks, would I agree to the Hon. Mr. Ferguson remaining in office as High Commissioner for Canada should I again come into office. May I say this, that if the Hon. Howard Ferguson, during four years of office in the United States as the representative of Canada had discharged his duties in the highly acceptable manner that Mr. Massey did, had he gained the esteem and regard of the Canadian people and of the British people to the degree to which Mr. Massey gained it in that time, I should certainly, had he been appointed to London at a time I came into office, have thought twice before I would have asked him immediately to forego that position. If the Hon. Howard Ferguson were to be asked by me to resign immediately, it would not be on the score of partisanship exhibited before the election, though heaven knows that no
man ever exhibited more in the way of partisanship; it would be for the manner in which he has discharged the duties of high commissioner since he has been in London.
In this connection I think I may as well proceed to see to what extent the present High Commissioner in London is reflecting the mind of the present administration. My right hon. friend says that the duty of the High Commissioner in London'-he repeated it this afternoon-is, first of all, to reflect the policies that are originated and initiated by the government of Canada. That is the first thing-to reflect the policies that are originated and initiated by the government. The second is to reflect the spirit and attitude of mind of the administration. The third thing is that he is practically a member of the administration. My right hon. friend has added to-night a fourth role which the High Commissioner in London fills, and that is that of civil servant.
I do not know how flattered the Hon. Howard Ferguson will be with his new title, but at any rate my right hon. friend has stressed it this evening.
Now I wish to read one or two utterances of the present high commissioner, and I shall ask my right hon. friend, because he and not the present high commissioner has to take the responsibility, how far the views expressed by the high commissioner reflect the policies of his administration, reflect the spirit and attitude of mind of the administration; how far the high commissioner is acting as a member of the administration, and how well he is qualifying himself to be continued in office as a civil servant.
My right hon. friend told us this afternoon that the Hon. Howard Ferguson was appointed on the 28th of November. As a matter of fact, he was not sworn in, I think, until some little time after that. He was sworn into office on the 18th of December, but he was appointed by order in council on the 2Sth of November. Now, between the date on which he was appointed by order in council and the date on which he was sworn in, the present High Commissioner for Canada in Great Britain gave a public address in which he outlined his conception of the aims and duties of the high commissioner. The address was delivered with that end in view. It was a public utterance, so that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister could not fail to understand to the full exactly what view the Hon. Howard Ferguson took of the appointment which had been given him on the 28th of November and to the fulfil-
Supply-External Affairs

ment of the duties of which he was formally sworn on the 18th of December. I will read from a Canadian Press report which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of December 5, and in other papers of the same date. I will read the account through and then ask my right hon. friend afterwards, if he will permit me, with respect to the policies and views therein set forth, how far they reflect the mind and the attitude of the present administration.
Before I read the statement of the present high commissioner's views as to his own duties and functions, let me remind the house of what was said by my right hon. friend only this afternoon in discussing another measure at the opening of the sitting. My right hon. friend was talking then of sovereign powers, of not interfering with each other's domestic affairs. He said that one country had no right to interfere with the affairs of another country, and he made a very strong point of that. Now I assume that in that particular he does not regard one rule or practice as existing for a country which is a foreign country and another and different rule and practice existing for a country which happens to be a nation within the British commonwealth of nations to which we belong. I would assume, at least, that he would expect any representative of the government of Canada to be as careful about not interfering in the internal affairs of another part of the British Empire as he would be about a representative of this country not interfering in the domestic affairs of some foreign nation, and particularly not interfering in the domestic affairs of Great Britain.
Last week the hon. member for Vegreville spoke with respect to conditions in Poland, and my right hon. friend then laid down the doctrine which should govern this country in discussing the internal affairs of other countries. This is what he said on May 8th last:
When you begin to discuss the internal government of a friendly power you are on very dangerous ground. It is not the duty of this Dominion to undertake to advise people how they should govern themselves. That is their business.
He also said:	.
There is an obligation upon us as a member of the League of Nations, and it is a rather serious obligation, not to reflect upon the other members of that league.
Now Great Britain is a member of the League of Nations as well as Canada and Poland, and the words which my right hon. friend used in reference to Poland I take it would in his mind foe equally applicable to Great Britain. Having made clear the position as he has stated it himself, I would ask my
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
right hon. friend to be prepared to tell us how far the expressions of view by his representative in London reflect the spirit of his administration and their policies:
Toronto, December i-A detail of his aims and ambitions as High Commissioner for Canada in London and a diagnosis of the ills which are now afflicting the British empire as a whole, and Canada and Great Britain in particular, was given by Premier G. Howard Ferguson, of Ontario, to the members of the Technical Service Council at their second annual dinner here to-night.
Remember, this was after Mr. Ferguson had been appointed high commissioner by order in council, but before he was formally sworn faithfully to discharge the duties of that office. Had the Prime Minister felt that these views did not reflect those of his administration, all he had to do was to say to his friend that he did not see very well how he could be sworn to office in view of his entertaining those particular views. In the absence of that step, we must assume that these are also the views of the Prime Minister:
''If I can," said Mr. Ferguson, "revive the invaluable stimulus that for centuries has been the basis of British progress and achievement, if I can contribute somewhat to direct the thought and endeavours of the British Isles toward cooperation with those portions of the empire outside the isles, if I can help to create a new attitude toward empire problems, I shall feel that I have been amply rewarded for some of the things that I leave behind me here in Canada, and for the efforts that I intend to make to accomplish my aims."
"I am not going over there to sell wheat. I am going to London with the hope that I may be able to do something to remould, or revise the contemporary spirit of the British people," said Mr. Ferguson.
"My observations over there are brief, and, perhaps, unreliable." Premier Ferguson said, "In the old country patriotic fervour, British persistence. British traditions, have to a large extent broken down. You all know the pride the Britisher has always taken in his country, in his production, in his position in the business and industrial world.
"Unfortunately the fact that they have tens of thousands of grown men that never did a day's work, the fact that they are paying what is termed the 'dole' to fifteen-year-old children and up, has contributed to the destruction of the morale of the British people. I think that is what is -wrong with Britain more than anything else.
"I can assure you that I never would have thought of leaving the happy hunting grounds, which I have enjoyed here for some time, if I did not think there was a real need for somebody to revive the old spirit of pride and self-respect for their country. I may not be the man, I doubt very much if I am. My spirit has been puddling round with the comparatively little things in the province of Ontario; and, when one goes out into the larger field-not only unknown to you-you are dealing not alone with national, but international affairs.

"Nevertheless, if I may use a clerical expression, ' when the call came' to me, and was pressed upon me, and it was pointed out that I might be of some service, I felt that, if I was to remain in the public service, that if I was imbued with the proper patriotism, that it was my duty to try. I am, therefore going to England to try to do something to revive that invaluable spirit."
Great Estates Ruined
Referring briefly to his recent visit in Great Britain the premier described "examples of where the extreme socialistic doctrine now prevailing in the motherland have led. It makes my heart bleed," he declared, "to see the great and traditional estates cut up and ruined by death duties, estates responsible for the greater and better part of our Canadian live stock, to quote only one instance of their value to us and the motherland. The education bill now before the English house raising the age of obligatory attendance at school to fifteen years, and providing for the subsidization of parents for loss of labour in this manner is another example of bad conditions now existent."
"Never in the history of living men has there been such a critical situation in the British Isles as at this moment and never has the whole people been so deeply concerned and stirred with national conditions as they are to-day. That, in my judgment, is the best evidence that they will, at a reasonably early stage, arise in their might and put a stop to this downward trend toward destruction."
I do not think I need read any more from that speech. I have read sufficient to indicate what in the. mind of the present high commissioner is his duty in the old land, his conception of the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite and of their attitude of mind with respect to those policies.
A few minutes ago my right hon. friend said he did not regard the. high commissioner as an ambassador or as having a diplomatic position. That being so I would ask him how it happens that he undertook to remind the high commissioner after that gentleman had made the speech I have read of what had happened to Sackville-West. Sackville-West was an ambassador who had been somewhat indiscreet in a letter he had written and as a result was recalled. My right hon. friend took occasion to administer a sharp rebuke or reprimand to his political friend and to say that he was so doing by way of example, indicating clearly that despite his present remarks in his view the position of high com-, missioner is supposed to carry with it some of the responsibilities of a diplomat, that the position in fact is diplomatic in character. Speaking of the reprimand by my right hon. friend and bearing in mind his conception of the high commissioner as a civil servant, I would remind the house that the occasion upon which the reprimand was administered was that of the opening of the Albany club,
a Tory political club, in the city of Toronto on January 6, after the high commissioner had been appointed by order in council and had been sworn to the duties of his office. On that particular occasion the Prime Minister himself in his speech reminded the audience that the Albany club was the very cradle of Conservatism in Canada. I should like to know from him whether he holds the view that as a civil servant Mr. Ferguson is to have the right of attending banquets at political clubs, is to be free to enunciate all kinds of view's; and in particular does my right hon. friend say that what was expressed by Mr. Ferguson in the address I have just read represents the policies of the government and the spirit of the present administration towards the problems of Great Britain? If those, statements do not represent the policies and spirit of the government I ask the Prime Minister what steps he purposes to take or what steps if any he has already taken to make clear to the British people that Mr. Ferguson in thus speaking did not express the ^views of the administration.

Bearing in mind the Prime Minister's statement that the high commissioner reflects the spirit and attitude of the administration, I ask if the spirit and attitude of the Conservative government in Canada towards Great Britain is as described in the following:
In the old country patriotic fervour, British persistence, British traditions, have to a large extent broken down. You all know the pride

the Britisher has always taken in his country, in his production, in his position in the business and industrial world.
Unfortunately the fact that they have tens of thousands of grown men that never did a day's work, the fact that they are paying what is termed the "dole" to fifteen-year old children and up. has contributed to the destruction of the morale of the British people.
Is that the view of the administration? Does my right hon. friend think this expression with regard to the British people by the high commissioner for Canada will gain for him any confidence on the part of the government or people of Great Britain? Does the Prime Minister think that the administration represented by the high commissioner, which keeps him in that position despite utterances of this character, will command any respect from any government in Great Britain or from the people of that country? Then he proceeds:
.... a real need for somebody to revive the old spirit of pride and self-respect for their country .... I am therefore going to England to try to do something to revive that invaluable spirit.
Then we come to another part, of the speech. At the time this utterance was made the British government had before it certain legislation dealing with educational matters. The high commissioner was not in doubt as to the existence of the bill or the stage which it had reached, because he said:
The education bill now before the English house raising the age of obligatory attendance at school to fifteen years and providing for the subsidization of parents for loss of labour in this manner is another example of bad conditions now existent.
May I ask the Prime Minister this question: If the High Commissioner for Great Britain, who represents the British government in this country, made a similar statement with regard to legislation before any of the provincial legislatures of Canada or before this parliament, would my right hon. friend remain silent and utter no protest, or would he ask for the recall of the high commissioner? I say there is nothing-and I agree with my right hon. friend in this- in connection with which a representative of one country must be more careful than interfering in the domestic affairs of another country. When the representative of Canada accredited to Great Britain deliberately endeavours to destroy legislation which is being promoted by the government to which he is being sent, surely the time has come when someone in the country should draw the attention of the ministry to the fact and place upon the ministry the responsibility for permitting that sort of thing to continue.

In what I am saying now I am not reflecting upon the present high commissioner. He has reflected upon himself, but I am concerned with the ministry of Canada. I am concerned with my right hon. friend and the attitude which he takes towards the representative of Canada in Great Britain. I say that unless he is prepared to endorse these sentiments he owes it to Great Britain to make some public explanation not only to this house but to Great Britain as well with respect to the attitude of his government in regard to these matters.

I am in a sense sorry
for the right hon. Prime Minister, but on the other hand he certainly has brought this calamity upon himself. I do not think the right hon. gentleman was fair to himself or to the position he occupies when he endeavoured this afternoon and to-night to reduce the status of the High Commissioner for Canada in Great Britain to that of the servant of a government, the tool of a party, instead of the representative of a whole country. I do not think that is a fair position to take.
My right hon. friend referred to the statute. That statute was passed in the old days when Canada was a colony and had not reached that equality of status of which my right hon. friend now is boasting, as I am. The language of the statute is specific. It says:
The high commissioner shall
(a) act as representative and resident agent of Canada in Great Britain, and in that capacity, execute such powers and perform such duties as are, from time to time, conferred upon and assigned to him by the governor in council.
Since then the various Imperial conferences have considered the status of the High Commissioner for Canada, and it has been decided that Great Britain should send a high commissioner here as we are sending a high commissioner to Great Britain. The high commissioners in London have been given high precedence at court and elsewhere, coming after the ambassadors. I repeat that the high commissioner represents the whole of Canada and all the people of this country. If we were to accept the views of the right hon. gentleman I am sure some of us would not feel at home when we went to London and visited the Canada building. Previously every Canadian thought he was at home there, but now he will have to be a Conservative and a supporter of the right hon. gentleman to have that feeling.
Mj' right hon. leader has referred to one of the numerous speeches made by the present high commissioner. I will not go as far as a
newspaper went sometime ago, after one of his outbursts at a banquet in England. That newspaper, which is not at all a supporter of the leader of the opposition, said, "Every time Mr. Ferguson speaks, Canada blushes." I would not go so far as to say that, but I will say that it relieves her dignity to some extent when the right hon. gentleman takes the stand that Mr. Ferguson speaks only for the government, that he speaks as a civil servant and for his party, and that he does not speak for me or for the rest of the people of Canada. It is a good thing that the people of Great Britain should know that we in this country who are not supporters of the right hon. gentleman do not share the views of the high commissioner as he has been expressing them to the people of Great Britain.
The office of High Commissioner for Canada in London is the highest in our diplomatic service. That view has been accepted by the people of Canada, and our representative there should act as a diplomat, as an ambassador, as the representative of one country to another. What are the duties of a diplomat? He has to use tact and judgment; he must be unobtrusive. I remember hearing Sir Esme Howard, who was a very distinguished British ambassador at Washington, speak before the Canadian Club in Ottawa. At that time he said, "Go everywhere in the world; you will not find any monument erected to a diplomat. We work in silence."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: That is hardly accurate.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
It is accurate. I quote another definition by another diplomat, Sir Edward Mallet, who was at one time British ambassador at Berlin. He said:
The world is a huge body clad in a garment of state. We diplomatists, studded all over the earth, are unobtrusive buttons which hold the garments together. As long as we perform this function satisfactorily we pass unnoticed, because the garments continue to sit properly. It is only when we break loose or come off that we become an object of attention or discussion.
The trouble with our High Commissioner in London is that he breaks loose, and that is why he is attracting such attention and so much discussion. And I know that my right hon. friend regrets it more than we do on this side of the house.
As my right hon. leader has noted, Sir William Clark, who occupies the same position in Canada, was appointed by a Conservative government, and he was retained in the office by the present Labour government.- I do not know whether he is still in office, but I know that the High Commissioner for Australia,
Supply-External Affairs

General Ryrie, who had been appointed by Mr. Bruce, was retained when the Labour government took office in that Dominion. I know also that the High Commissioner for New Zealand kept office after Mr. Coates had resigned and had been replaced by the present government there. My right 'hon. friend opposite seems to foe the only one who holds the view that the high commissioner must be his servant, or tool, or supporter, or by whatever term you choose to describe him, instead of being the representative of the country
I saw in the newspapers yesterday the statement of an admirer of our representative in Britain to the effect that he was selling Canada to England. Well, I must admit that his methods have more the appearance of salesmanship than of statesmanship. I do not think there is any doubt about that. My right hon. friend made reference to Sir Charles Tupper's having taken part in an election in Canada while he was high commissioner. Surely my right hon. friend does not consider this desirable. Surely our representative in Britain to-day ought to be the representative of all Canadians and not merely of a party. I do not think it is fair to take that stand, and even if it was done in the past it should not be done now.
During the last general election I had the pleasure of visiting some constituencies in the province of Ontario. Do not blame me for anything that may have happened, for I believe that we won in most of the constituencies in which I appeared-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: You picked them with care.	[DOT]

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for having come there.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I knew the hon. gentleman would say that. I anticipated the remark, for I believe he has said that I rather helped him. However, Mr. Ferguson took exception to a minister representing Quebec going into Ontario and addressing the people of that province. May I suggest that a federal minister is minister for the whole Dominion of Canada, and therefore I had more business speaking in Ontario on federal matters than Mr. Ferguson has speaking in Britain on British matters.
Before concluding, I wish to join with my leader in paying tribute to Mr. Massey. Mr. Massey was not the tool of a party while he represented Canada in Washington. I remember attending a dinner of the Pilgrims Society

in New York in honour of Mr. Massey. There were five hundred representative Americans present and they had invited twenty public men of Canada, more than half of whom were Conservatives. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Fisheries was one of the guests, and if he were here he could bear me out when I speak of the high esteem, the affection and the respect in which Mr. Massey was held in the United States of America. Indeed, I have never heard a eulogy so eloquently expressed as the praises of Mr. Massey by Canon Cody of Toronto, who is certainly not a Liberal and was not politically a friend of Mr. IVfassey. My best wish for Mr. Ferguson would be that some day he might merit the same tribute.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition, in his remarks, read from the report of a speech made by the High Commissioner in London, in which he is represented as having said that he was not in the old country to sell wheat. My memory is not particularly good, but when that speech was quoted, my mind went back to a despatch which I saw in a number of newspapers in which I observed that the hon. gentleman who holds the important office of High Commissioner for Canada in London was supposed to have visited Rome for the purpose of attending a conference, in connection, I presume, with the sale of wheat. It appears, therefore, that Mr. Ferguson, between the time he made that speech in Toronto and the time at which he arrived in Rome to attend that important conference, must have changed his mind or else have received instructions from the Prime Minister intimating that he had certain duties to discharge in regard to the business of this country which would take him to that conference. The ex-Minister of Justice also referred to the fact that Mr. Ferguson had expressed disapproval of a minister in the Liberal cabinet, representing the province of Quebec, going into Ontario and taking part in the last federal election. Mr. Ferguson evidently has also changed his mind with respect to Quebec ministers; because in a despatch which I noticed in the Toronto Mail and Empire of April 2, 1931, I find the following :
Pope's apostolic blessing is bestowed on Ferguson.
That is the heading, and the despatch is by George Hambleton, Canadian Press staff writer. The article reads:
Rome, April 1.-Hon. G. Howard Ferguson, Canadian High Commission to London, who is attending the world wheat conference here, and Mrs. Ferguson, to-day were received by the pope in private audience.

Supply-External Ajjairs
"It was merely a courtesy call," Mr. Ferguson said afterwards to the Canadian Press. Later he would pay his respects to His Holiness on behalf of the Dominion, Mr. Ferguson said.
Mr. and Mrs. Ferguson were presented to the pope by G. A. D. Ogilvie-Forbes, Charge d'Affaires of the British Ministry to the Holy See.
The chief delegate of the Argentine to the world wheat conference. Tomas LeBreton, who is Argentine Ambassador to Paris, was also presented to the pope to-day.
His Holiness discussed Canada in a most cordial and interested manner, with Mr. and Mrs. Ferguson, and imparted an apostolic benediction before they left.
We are all glad that the high commissioner, after despatching his business in Rome, had the courtesy to call upon His Holiness, who graciously bestowed upon him the apostolic blessing. I am sure that you, Mr. Chairman, as well as I, after following Mr. Ferguson's political career in Ontario

and I am bound to say that there is much about him that I admire, for he is a bonny fighter and I admire a fighter-must be glad that, as I say, he had the courtesy to call upon the pope. I might say, on behalf of a certain section of the province of Nova Scotia, that I am delighted to think he went and saw the pope and got his blessing. But I wonder whether, before he called upon His Holiness, he also got the Prime. Minister's benediction.
Now what is the reaction in Canada to Mr. Ferguson's visit? On April 3 the Toronto Globe published an editorial under the caption. An Awkward Situation. I quote the following:
Now the fat is in the fire. Canada's High Commissioner in London has received the blessing of Has Holiness the Pope. There is nothing unusual in this. Other eminent men from many countries have been recipients of the same attention while in Rome. But the point lies in Mr. Ferguson's fraternal affiliations in this country in the days before he ceased being a politician and became a diplomat.
After listening to the remarks of the Prime Minister I am convinced that Mr. Ferguson is still a politician and not a diplomat. The article continues:
It is unfortunate that this incident occurred just after the grand lodges of the province have held their annual meetings. But surely something can be done about it. In view of this news from Rome, can a man who has been familiar with the inner circles of the order be honoured any more? The only official and prompt action that seems possible just now is to change the password. It seems improbable that a former high official of the lodge, fresh from an audience with the pope, should have the daring to present himself before the tyler; but Mr. Ferguson is nothing if not courageous, and may try it.
The question to be decided is wdiether the present High Commissioner for Canada, former Premier of Ontario and honoured member of
an influential order, is making progress or slipping backward. This will be answered in different ways by the people of the province. Grand knights and members of the Knights of Columbus may be depended upon to approve Mr. Ferguson's action; to them it will look like a gain. But the grand masters and the rank and file of the other order will think otherwise. It will be hard for them to arrive at a satisfactory and at the same time diplomatic decision.
There is no question but that Mr. Ferguson has "gone over to Rome," but he was dealing with the wheat problem. He has bent the knee before and been blessed by the head of a church that is known to have no great friendship for the order. This cannot be denied, as other people were present. Why did the high commissioner create such a situation? Probably because when in Rome he followed the example of other distinguished diplomats. And in the splendour of the Vatican he may have forgotten temporarily about old days in Ontario politics.
Let us hope he did. That article is from the Toronto Globe, but perhaps I should give the other side of the question. It may be said that the Toronto Globe is not very friendly to Mr. Ferguson, but I hold in my hand a paper, the editor of which is good enough to send copies to all members of this house, no matter what may be their politics or religion. This is The Sentinel.

Hon. G. Howard Ferguson's visit to the pope, and getting the papa! blessing, will come as a shock to the Orangemen of Canada.
The blessing presages disaster for the high commissioner, as in numerous other cases. The Spanish armada set sail with the pope's blessing. and see what happened to that. Innumerable other cases could be cited in which the pope's blessing preceded calamities to its recipients.
It will be said that diplomatic precedent required the Orange ex-Premier of Ontario to visit the pontiff. That will not go down with the Orange lodges in Canada. It would not have caused a rupture of any kind if Mr. Ferguson had left Rome without seeing the pope.
I do not suppose the pope would have become ill. The article continues:
One sure thing is that he was not thinking of his Orange friends back home when he paid his homage to the head of Romanism. There is, of course, no violation of his Orange obligation in getting the blessing of the pope, but to seek it is repugnant to every instinct of a true Orangeman.

This is the statement of a paper which has supported Mr. Ferguson for many years; this is what they think of Mr. Ferguson's actions while acting as high commissioner in London.
The amount of this vote this year is $132,260 as compared with $117,260 for last year, an increase of $15,000. We have been told that the government is economizing because of the financial conditions in this country, but here we are faced with an increase of $15,000. The increase includes an addition of $2,000 to the salary of the Hon. Mr. Ferguson. Apart from any criticism which might be made of Mr. Ferguson, the fact remains that under present day conditions he should not receive an increase in salary. I object to Mr. Ferguson's receiving that extra $2,000 -when there are other important matters which should be looked after. Civil servants are being dismissed people are out of employment, public works are being curtailed, and I object to and protest against this increase. What was Mr. Ferguson's salary, before this increase was granted?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The statute provides for a salary of $10,000, but an additional $2,000 has been paid for many years. The position of high commissioner necessitates his residing in London. There is no residence in London as there is in Washington, and the increase is to provide something in the way of accommodation. No doubt something will have to be done with regard to a residence in London. The high commissionership must not be left open for rich men alone, but unless some provision of this sort is made, only rich men can accept it. To one having an income of $900,000 or $1,000,000 per year, the office was worth three or four hundred thousand annually because the incumbent does not have to pay income tax. Something has to 'be provided in the case of men in moderate circumstances. Since the days of Sir Charles Tupper it has not been found necessary to make this provision, until the present instance. The office in Paris carries with it a residence at a very low rental. It was first rented immediately after the war, and the minister told me that the rent was something between one and two thousand dollars. When the estimates were being prepared a cable was sent to the minister to make certain about that rental.
So far as the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) is concerned, I suppose the correct answer to his remarks would be that contained in the school textbooks: When at Rome do as the Romans do.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

The hon. member for
Quebec-East (Mr. Lapointe) has been singularly unfair in his remarks, more so than he would like us on this side to be. I said that Mr. King was a civil servant.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I meant to say Mr. Ferguson. It is long since my right hon. friend was a civil servant.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman should not let his animosity extend so far. First, may I suggest the statute provides:
The high commissioner shall act as representative and resident agent of Canada in Great Britain.
He represents all Canada, just as I frequently used to say that the right hon. gentleman himself was not only Prime Minister and leader of his party, but leader of the House of Commons; just as the government is the government of Canada and not the government of a party. So Mr. Ferguson under the statute is the representative and resident agent of Canada in Great Britain. I think it was not cricket for my hon. frieud to try to assert that I had lowered Mr. Ferguson's status by referring to him as I presently shall again, as a civil servant. But his position is as the representative in Great Britain of Canada, of all provinces, of all Canadians, of all classes and creeds. He is the Canadian representative, and no one would more quickly than Mr. Ferguson himself disown the thought that in that position he represented the party. That is number one.
The second is:
The high commissioner shall, in that capacity, execute such powers and perform such duties as are, from time to time, conferred upon and assigned to him by the governor in council.
To that extent be is the instrument of the government to do what the government by order in council directs to be done. The third is:
The high commissioner shall take the charge, supervision and control of the immigration offices and agencies in Great Britain, under the Minister of Immigration and Colonization.

Supply-External Affairs
There his chief is the Minister of Immigration; there his direction is from the Minister of Immigration; there he is to all intents and purposes a deputy minister with regard to that particular work. The fourth is:
The high commissioner shall carry out such instructions as he, from time to time, receives from the governor in council respecting the commercial, financial and general interests of Canada in Great Britain and elsewhere.
I think my hon. friend will now agree that in the first instance the gentleman in question represents Canada; second, he is in the position of a civil servant, and I am using that word in its proper sense, in that he is carrying into effect the directions received from time to time by (a) the governor in council, and (b) the Minister of Immigration. An ambassador, a minister from Great Britain, is a civil servant and is classified as such.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: When the term is used, therefore, in that sense, as I used it, I think the hon. gentleman was not quite fair in endeavouring to have it appear that the expression had been applied to the High Commissioner in some derogatory sense. For no higher praise can be given to any man than that he is serving the state faithfully as a civil servant. The permanent civil servants of Britain are the men who have maintained the continuity of her policy and her supremacy for instance, in finance, commerce, and so forth.
